weaknesses: The repeated claim of an unbiased estimator is stronger than the established result. Theorem 4.1 assumes exact population drifts; substituting learned neural drifts introduces approximation and statistical errors. No finite-sample unbiasedness guarantee, consistency result, or error bound supports the practical estimator. Removing a terminal-distribution approximation does not eliminate these other sources of bias.

The pointwise mutual information extension is mathematically incorrect. Equation (22) is necessarily nonnegative, whereas PMI can be negative. For example, a standard bivariate Gaussian with correlation 0.5 has PMI approximately -0.856 at (1,-1). The stochastic-integral term in Girsanov’s formula cannot generally be discarded after conditioning on both endpoints. This invalidates the claimed PMI estimator, although it does not invalidate the averaged MI identity.

The training procedure leaves an important endpoint singularity unresolved. Algorithm 2 samples time uniformly and uses unweighted targets containing 1/(1-t). Even with independent standard-normal endpoints and epsilon=1, the minimum conditional regression error is 1/(1-t), whose time integral diverges. Any clipping, weighting, or alternative parameterization used to handle this must be specified and its consequences examined.

The decisive comparison with prior diffusion estimation is missing: MINDE is absent from the image experiments, while the low-dimensional results show broadly comparable performance. Consequently, the practical benefit of the bridge formulation and removal of MINDE’s terminal KL term remains unestablished. Image comparisons also use a roughly 27-million-parameter model requiring 6 or 18 A100 GPU-hours, versus at most two hours for discriminative baselines, without controlling model capacity or computational budget.

The evidence for complex, high-dimensional estimation is limited to synthetic Gaussian and rectangle images generated from low-dimensional latent variables. These experiments do not establish performance at high intrinsic dimensionality or on realistic data. Moreover, Figure 1 shows substantial remaining underestimation on Gaussian images: approximately 7.5–8 nats when the true MI is 10.

Important ablations and uncertainty analyses are missing. The claimed benefit of sharing the two drift networks is not demonstrated against separate networks, epsilon is fixed without sensitivity analysis, and sample-size scaling is unexplored. Low-dimensional tables report means without variability, while the image results use only three InfoBridge seeds to construct 99% asymptotic confidence intervals.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing repository URLs in Appendix B and an inconsistent description of baseline objectives: Appendix B.2 states that MINE, NWJ, and InfoNCE were trained with MAE loss despite previously defining their distinct variational objectives.
